title: Shagufta Ali Reveals She Hid Stage 3 Breast Cancer for Years, Fearing Bollywood Would Stop Calling
excerpt: The veteran TV actress opens up about her cancer survival, financial ruin and the industry stigma that forced her into silence about her diagnosis.
body:
• Veteran actress Shagufta Ali has revealed she kept her Stage 3 breast cancer diagnosis secret for years, fearing the industry would stop offering her work.
  • She underwent major surgery and chemotherapy while continuing to shoot, travelling to Dubai just 17 days after surgery with a cushion strapped to her chest.
  • The actress says she exhausted all her savings covering medical expenses and household costs as the sole earner, eventually selling her jewellery and car.
  • Her story highlights the persistent stigma around illness in the Indian entertainment industry, where health disclosures can quietly end careers.

The Silence That Survival Demanded

Shagufta Ali has appeared in dozens of beloved Hindi television shows over a career spanning more than three decades — from Saans to Sanjivani: A Medical Boon, Madhubala – Ek Ishq Ek Junoon and Bepannaah. But for years, she carried a secret that weighed heavier than any on-screen role.

https://x.com/htshowbiz/status/2081179761968361581

In a candid interview with Siddharth Kannan, the actress revealed that she was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer during the peak of her career. She kept the diagnosis hidden from virtually everyone in the industry, sharing it only with a handful of close friends.

"Uss zamaane mein batana nahi tha... phir wahi darr, dara diya ki kaam nahi milega. Industry waale aisa behave karte hain."

— Shagufta Ali, on why she hid her cancer diagnosis

The fear was not abstract. Shagufta described an industry culture where illness was treated as a liability — where the unspoken rule was to stay silent or risk being quietly replaced. "Don't talk about it. Don't speak about it," she recalled being told. The message was clear: disclosure meant the phone would stop ringing.

Surgery, Chemotherapy and a Cushion on a Flight to Dubai

Despite the severity of her diagnosis, Shagufta continued working through treatment. She underwent major surgery to remove the tumour and endured multiple rounds of chemotherapy, which she described as "getting a new birth every time."

Just 17 days after her surgery — against her doctor's explicit warnings — she boarded a flight to Dubai with a cushion pressed against her chest to protect the still-healing surgical site. She was going to shoot for her show. "The doctor had clearly told me, you will do it at your own risk," she recalled. During this period, she was juggling three to four shows simultaneously, plus film shoots.

Financial Devastation

Cancer was not the only blow. Shagufta revealed that she was the sole earning member of her household, supporting her aged mother and other dependents. Her savings — accumulated over decades of steady work — were gradually consumed by medical bills, household expenses and the extended period of reduced work that followed.

Eventually, she sold her jewellery and her car. She draws the line at her home. "People ask, didn't you have savings? I had plenty. But when you're the only earner and everything — illnesses, daily expenses, the household — falls on you, it gets exhausted."

She now travels to doctors' appointments and work in auto-rickshaws, a far cry from her years as a lead on prime-time television. When the industry body CINTAA offered financial help earlier, she declined, saying the amount offered was insufficient to make a meaningful difference.

A Wider Problem in Indian Entertainment

Shagufta's story is not unique, but it is unusually frank. Indian cinema and television have seen several actors — from Irrfan Khan and Rishi Kapoor to more recently Hina Khan — navigate cancer diagnoses with varying degrees of openness. But the entertainment industry's informal hiring practices mean that character actors and supporting cast members lack the safety net that star power can provide.

There is no industry-wide health insurance mandate in Indian television production. Actors on daily soaps typically work as independent contractors with no benefits, sick leave or job protection. For someone like Shagufta — respected but not a marquee name — disclosing cancer could be career-ending in ways it would not be for a superstar.

Looking Ahead

Shagufta says she is now a cancer survivor and is speaking publicly for the first time about her full experience, partly to break the stigma that forced her silence. Her last significant role was in Bepannaah, and she continues to seek work in an industry that, by her account, has yet to reckon with how it treats its most vulnerable members.
nri_angle: Shagufta Ali's story resonates with diaspora audiences who grew up watching her on Indian television and highlights the lack of financial safety nets for working actors in the industry.
